Mi alzo: reflexive verbs

Italian adds a small pronoun where English usually doesn't. \"I get up\" is mi alzo (literally \"I raise myself\"): a little pronoun before the verb, then the verb conjugated the way you already know (alzare → alzo, vestire → vesto).

alzarsi (to get up)vestirsi (to get dressed)
iomi alzomi vesto
tuti alziti vesti
lui, leisi alzasi veste
noici alziamoci vestiamo
voivi alzatevi vestite
lorosi alzanosi vestono

What to watch out for:

  • the pronoun is mi, ti, si, and it goes before the conjugated verb; the subject is usually left out: mi alzo is enough;
  • we → ci, you (plural) → vi;
  • si is used for he, she and also for they: si alza, si alzano;
  • in the infinitive, the pronoun is attached to the end, replacing the final -e: alzare → alzarsi = to get up, svegliarsi = to wake up.

You already know one: Come ti chiami? — Mi chiamo Anna. That's the verb chiamarsi (literally \"to call oneself\").

Non mi sveglio presto.I don't wake up early.

Non goes before the pronoun: non mi alzo = I don't get up. And Italian says mi lavo i denti (I brush my teeth, literally \"I wash myself the teeth\"): the article, not a possessive like \"my\".

", "

Che ore sono? Telling time

To ask the time: Che ore sono? (you'll also hear Che ora è?). To answer, Italian says \"they are the eight\": sono le otto. The word ore (hours) is understood: you don't say it.

unoduetrequattrocinquesei
789101112
setteottonovedieciundicidodici
It's…In Italian
8:00Sono le otto.
8:10Sono le otto e dieci.
8:15Sono le otto e un quarto.
8:30Sono le otto e mezza (you'll also hear e mezzo).
8:45Sono le nove meno un quarto.
1:00È l'una.
12:00 noonÈ mezzogiorno.
12:00 midnightÈ mezzanotte.

The trap: one o'clock, noon and midnight are singular (è l'una, è mezzogiorno). All the other hours are plural (sono le due, sono le sette).

At what time?

A che ora…? = at what time? In the answer, a merges with the article of the hour: alle sette, all'una. But noon and midnight have no article: a mezzogiorno, a mezzanotte.

A che ora ti alzi? — Mi alzo alle sette e un quarto.What time do you get up? — I get up at a quarter past seven.

For the parts of the day: la mattina (the morning), il pomeriggio (the afternoon), la sera (the evening), la notte (the night). To be precise about a time: le otto di sera, eight in the evening (8 p.m.).

title: My day
topic: reflexive verbs in the present; telling time
why: First lesson of the unit "My everyday life": after a whole unit on the regular present, the learner reuses those endings to describe their day. Reflexive verbs only add a small pronoun to endings already known, which allows a slow pace; telling time brings two targeted traps: the plural (sono le otto) and alle sette.
